The traditional lingua franca of the area is Avar, which is still taught as a school
subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,
which is also the medium of education in Tsez schools. Prior to the break-up of the
Soviet Union, the Russo-Georgian armed conflict, and the closure of the border,
economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

State of research

Although some basic material on Tsez is provided in Dirr (1909), the first
reasonably detailed published sketch of the language is Bokarev (1959); a more up-to-
date sketch is provided by Alekseev & Radžabov (1989). The fullest monograph

is under preparation by Polinsky & Comrie (in prep). The latter will also include a full
bibliography of earlier work. Xalilov (1999) is a dictionary of about 7500 entries, the
first and so far only substantial dictionary of the language.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by

(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl

Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by

others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where

1.3.
Sociolinguistic situation

Tsez has the official status of an unwritten language. A primer for use in schools
has been prepared (Alekseev 1993; Alekseev, Radžabov & Abdulaev 2003), but seems
to be little used. Occasional pieces in Tsez appear in the local newspaper Didojskie vesti
<http://cunta.ru/didoyskievesti>, as well as occasional small publications, e.g. of
poetry. But by far the most substantial collection of Tsez texts is the folklore anthology
(Abdulaev & Abdullaev 2010). All of these, like the dictionary (Xalilov 1999), make
use of adaptations of Avar Cyrillic orthography (see section 2.2); Avar and Tsez
phonologies are typologically quite close.

The traditional lingua franca of the area is Avar, which is still taught as a school
subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,
which is also the medium of education in Tsez schools. Prior to the break-up of the
Soviet Union, the Russo-Georgian armed conflict, and the closure of the border,
economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

Tsez is the main language of everyday communication for Tsez speakers in the
Tsunta District, and children grow up speaking it as their first and, at least until
recently, only language before entering school. But two recent factors have made
Russian more salient in village life: accessibility to modern media, and

Georgian has provided a substantial number of nouns reflecting the pre-technological

loans, including internationalisms. Especially earlier loans from Russian often show

doktor), gazit, gazjat, gazijat ‘newspaper’ (Russian gazeta), pabrika ‘factory’ (Russian

Loans from Russian also include discourse particles, especially in slang.

More comparative work is needed before loans from other Tsezic or from Andic
languages can be consistently identified, but bišon ‘hundred’ is clearly a loan from an
Andic language (Nikolayev & Starostin 1994: 588).

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

3.4.
Pronouns

Morphologically, Tsez has distinct classes of personal pronouns (first and second
person only — third person pronouns are expressed as demonstratives, že ‘he, she, it’,
žedi ‘they’), demonstrative pronouns, and interrogative pronouns.

The first and second person singular pronouns are unusual in having a single
form for both absolutive and ergative: di ‘I’, mi ‘you’. The oblique stem of ‘I’ is da:-,
and that of ‘you’ is debe- before a syllable-final consonant (e.g. lative debe-r), dow-
before a syllable-initial consonant (e.g. apud.essive dow-de). Both pronouns have
irregular genitive 1: dej ‘my’, debi ‘your’ (the genitive 2 is regular: da:-z, debe-z).

The first and second person plural pronouns eli ‘we’, meži ‘you-all’ have the
regular absolutive versus ergative distinction; they also make a gender distinction in
oblique cases, with stems I elu-, mežu-, II-IV ela-, meža-. In addition to the regular
genitives elu-s, ela-s, elu-z, ela-z, mežu-s, mežu-z, meža-s, meža-z, they also have
special forms genitive 1 eli, meži, genitive 2 eli-z, meži-z, used where the possessor is a

impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

The traditional lingua franca of the area is Avar, which is still taught as a school
subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,

economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by

material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where

State of research

Although some basic material on Tsez is provided in Dirr (1909), the first
reasonably detailed published sketch of the language is Bokarev (1959); a more up-to-

is under preparation by Polinsky & Comrie (in prep). The latter will also include a full
bibliography of earlier work. Xalilov (1999) is a dictionary of about 7500 entries, the
first and so far only substantial dictionary of the language.

Tsez has the official status of an unwritten language. A primer for use in schools

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,

impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

The first and second person singular pronouns are unusual in having a single

and that of ‘you’ is debe- before a syllable-final consonant (e.g. lative debe-r), dow-
before a syllable-initial consonant (e.g. apud.essive dow-de). Both pronouns have
irregular genitive 1: dej ‘my’, debi ‘your’ (the genitive 2 is regular: da:-z, debe-z).

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

Sociolinguistic situation

Tsez has the official status of an unwritten language. A primer for use in schools
has been prepared (Alekseev 1993; Alekseev, Radžabov & Abdulaev 2003), but seems

poetry. But by far the most substantial collection of Tsez texts is the folklore anthology
(Abdulaev & Abdullaev 2010). All of these, like the dictionary (Xalilov 1999), make
use of adaptations of Avar Cyrillic orthography (see section 2.2); Avar and Tsez
phonologies are typologically quite close.

The traditional lingua franca of the area is Avar, which is still taught as a school
subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,
which is also the medium of education in Tsez schools. Prior to the break-up of the
Soviet Union, the Russo-Georgian armed conflict, and the closure of the border,
economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

3.4.
Pronouns

Morphologically, Tsez has distinct classes of personal pronouns (first and second
person only — third person pronouns are expressed as demonstratives, že ‘he, she, it’,
žedi ‘they’), demonstrative pronouns, and interrogative pronouns.

The first and second person singular pronouns are unusual in having a single
form for both absolutive and ergative: di ‘I’, mi ‘you’. The oblique stem of ‘I’ is da:-,
and that of ‘you’ is debe- before a syllable-final consonant (e.g. lative debe-r), dow-
before a syllable-initial consonant (e.g. apud.essive dow-de). Both pronouns have
irregular genitive 1: dej ‘my’, debi ‘your’ (the genitive 2 is regular: da:-z, debe-z).

Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by

Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no

Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

3.4.
Pronouns

Morphologically, Tsez has distinct classes of personal pronouns (first and second
person only — third person pronouns are expressed as demonstratives, že ‘he, she, it’,
žedi ‘they’), demonstrative pronouns, and interrogative pronouns.

The first and second person singular pronouns are unusual in having a single
form for both absolutive and ergative: di ‘I’, mi ‘you’. The oblique stem of ‘I’ is da:-,
and that of ‘you’ is debe- before a syllable-final consonant (e.g. lative debe-r), dow-
before a syllable-initial consonant (e.g. apud.essive dow-de). Both pronouns have
irregular genitive 1: dej ‘my’, debi ‘your’ (the genitive 2 is regular: da:-z, debe-z).

The first and second person plural pronouns eli ‘we’, meži ‘you-all’ have the
regular absolutive versus ergative distinction; they also make a gender distinction in
oblique cases, with stems I elu-, mežu-, II-IV ela-, meža-. In addition to the regular
genitives elu-s, ela-s, elu-z, ela-z, mežu-s, mežu-z, meža-s, meža-z, they also have
special forms genitive 1 eli, meži, genitive 2 eli-z, meži-z, used where the possessor is a
close group, typically a family; compare eli enij ‘our mother’ with elu-s ˁa

Sociolinguistic situation

Tsez has the official status of an unwritten language. A primer for use in schools
has been prepared (Alekseev 1993; Alekseev, Radžabov & Abdulaev 2003), but seems

use of adaptations of Avar Cyrillic orthography (see section 2.2); Avar and Tsez
phonologies are typologically quite close.

The traditional lingua franca of the area is Avar, which is still taught as a school
subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,
which is also the medium of education in Tsez schools. Prior to the break-up of the
Soviet Union, the Russo-Georgian armed conflict, and the closure of the border,
economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

Tsez is the main language of everyday communication for Tsez speakers in the
Tsunta District, and children grow up speaking it as their first and, at least until

1.4.
State of research

Although some basic material on Tsez is provided in Dirr (1909), the first
reasonably detailed published sketch of the language is Bokarev (1959); a more up-to-
date sketch is provided by Alekseev & Radžabov (1989). The fullest monograph
grammar to date is Imnajšvili (1963), while a grammar meeting contemporary standards
is under preparation by Polinsky & Comrie (in prep). The latter will also include a full
bibliography of earlier work. Xalilov (1999) is a dictionary of about 7500 entries, the
first and so far only substantial dictionary of the language.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.4.
State of research

Although some basic material on Tsez is provided in Dirr (1909), the first
reasonably detailed published sketch of the language is Bokarev (1959); a more up-to-
date sketch is provided by Alekseev & Radžabov (1989). The fullest monograph
grammar to date is Imnajšvili (1963), while a grammar meeting contemporary standards
is under preparation by Polinsky & Comrie (in prep). The latter will also include a full
bibliography of earlier work. Xalilov (1999) is a dictionary of about 7500 entries, the
first and so far only substantial dictionary of the language.

Prosody

Kibrik & Kodzasov (1990: 329) and Nikolayev & Starostin (1994: 115) note the

Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

Tsez has the official status of an unwritten language. A primer for use in schools
has been prepared (Alekseev 1993; Alekseev, Radžabov & Abdulaev 2003), but seems
to be little used. Occasional pieces in Tsez appear in the local newspaper Didojskie vesti

poetry. But by far the most substantial collection of Tsez texts is the folklore anthology
(Abdulaev & Abdullaev 2010). All of these, like the dictionary (Xalilov 1999), make
use of adaptations of Avar Cyrillic orthography (see section 2.2); Avar and Tsez
phonologies are typologically quite close.

The traditional lingua franca of the area is Avar, which is still taught as a school
subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,
which is also the medium of education in Tsez schools. Prior to the break-up of the
Soviet Union, the Russo-Georgian armed conflict, and the closure of the border,
economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no

there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

Morphologically, Tsez has distinct classes of personal pronouns (first and second
person only — third person pronouns are expressed as demonstratives, že ‘he, she, it’,
žedi ‘they’), demonstrative pronouns, and interrogative pronouns.

The first and second person singular pronouns are unusual in having a single
form for both absolutive and ergative: di ‘I’, mi ‘you’. The oblique stem of ‘I’ is da:-,
and that of ‘you’ is debe- before a syllable-final consonant (e.g. lative debe-r), dow-
before a syllable-initial consonant (e.g. apud.essive dow-de). Both pronouns have
irregular genitive 1: dej ‘my’, debi ‘your’ (the genitive 2 is regular: da:-z, debe-z).

Sociolinguistic situation

Tsez has the official status of an unwritten language. A primer for use in schools
has been prepared (Alekseev 1993; Alekseev, Radžabov & Abdulaev 2003), but seems
to be little used. Occasional pieces in Tsez appear in the local newspaper Didojskie vesti

poetry. But by far the most substantial collection of Tsez texts is the folklore anthology
(Abdulaev & Abdullaev 2010). All of these, like the dictionary (Xalilov 1999), make
use of adaptations of Avar Cyrillic orthography (see section 2.2); Avar and Tsez
phonologies are typologically quite close.

The traditional lingua franca of the area is Avar, which is still taught as a school
subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,
which is also the medium of education in Tsez schools. Prior to the break-up of the
Soviet Union, the Russo-Georgian armed conflict, and the closure of the border,
economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.

1.3.
Sociolinguistic situation

Tsez has the official status of an unwritten language. A primer for use in schools
has been prepared (Alekseev 1993; Alekseev, Radžabov & Abdulaev 2003), but seems
to be little used. Occasional pieces in Tsez appear in the local newspaper Didojskie vesti
<http://cunta.ru/didoyskievesti>, as well as occasional small publications, e.g. of
poetry. But by far the most substantial collection of Tsez texts is the folklore anthology
(Abdulaev & Abdullaev 2010). All of these, like the dictionary (Xalilov 1999), make
use of adaptations of Avar Cyrillic orthography (see section 2.2); Avar and Tsez
phonologies are typologically quite close.

The traditional lingua franca of the area is Avar, which is still taught as a school
subject in Tsez schools. However, the younger generation is more fluent in Russian,
which is also the medium of education in Tsez schools. Prior to the break-up of the
Soviet Union, the Russo-Georgian armed conflict, and the closure of the border,
economic ties with the neighboring Georgian province of Kakhetia meant that there was
also some knowledge of Georgian in the Tsez community; nowadays, there is no
impetus to acquire or maintain competence in Georgian. At the end of the 20th century
there were still a few elderly monolingual speakers of Tsez.

Tsez is the main language of everyday communication for Tsez speakers in the
Tsunta District, and children grow up speaking it as their first and, at least until
recently, only language before entering school. But two recent factors have made

1.2.
Dialects

The usually accepted subdivision of Tsez dialects follows that proposed by
Imnajšvili (1963: 9–10), which recognizes a primary distinction between the Sagada
(soƛ’o) dialect and the rest, which in turn are divided into Kidero (kidiro), Shaytl
(ešiƛ’), Asakh (asaq), Shapikh (šapiħ), and Elbok (elboq’) — the names in parentheses
are the Tsez versions. The Mokok (newo) dialect is, however, sufficiently different from
Kidero to be considered a separate dialect. The Sagada dialect diverges enough from the
others to impair mutual intelligibility, and Sagada speakers need to make
accommodations in interaction with speakers of other dialects. The other dialects are all
mutually intelligible, and none has noticeably greater prestige than any other. The
material in this article follows the Tsebari (ceboru) subdialect of Asakh, except where
otherwise specified.
